name: Most Muscular pose

image.caption: Mohammed Daood MoDaood most muscular stage pose

lead: The Most Muscular pose is one of the mandatory poses in men's bodybuilding competition, where competitors flex the whole body to show as much muscle size as possible. It makes the physique look bigger and fuller on stage and in photos.
Lifters also use it informally, and forum members mention hitting it as a gym joke or flexing check.

paras: Competitors hit the pose during the mandatory round of a show and in the posedown; Wikipedia lists it alongside front and back lat spreads, double biceps, side chest, side triceps, abdominals and thighs. Lifters practise posing to show muscle off better.
Intense isometric contraction can cause cramping and, for people with blood pressure issues, strain; otherwise risk is low.

angle.text: Posing technique changes how developed a physique looks without changing the muscle itself, so practising it is part of presenting a physique well.

lead: The Most Muscular pose is a men-only mandatory pose in bodybuilding competition, listed alongside front lat spread, rear lat spread, front and back double biceps, side chest, side triceps, abdominals and thighs.[1] Competitors also perform a choreographed routine and a posedown.[1]

The pose is designed to display overall muscle mass, so its appearance payoff is making existing muscle look larger and more developed to judges and cameras.[1] A lifter on T Nation noted that scapular control, moving the shoulder blades out to spread the lats and in and up to push the traps up, matters for the pose.[2]
infobox: Front double biceps, side chest, abdominals and thighs

paras: Most Muscular is among the mandatory poses and applies to men only.[1] Open bodybuilders are larger than men's physique competitors, whose judging relies mainly on front and back poses.[1]
T Nation members mention the pose in jokes and as a way to flex in the gym.[2][3] One forum post discusses controlling the scapulae to flare the lats and raise the traps for it.[2]

lore.intro: On T Nation the pose appears mostly as a humorous flex.[3]
